topic: Andhra Movement & Formation of Andhra Pradesh

items.title: Roots of the Andhra Movement (1913–1950)
items.body:
### Why Telugu speakers wanted their own province

**In one line:** Telugu districts inside the Tamil-dominated Madras Presidency began demanding a separate Andhra province as early as 1913.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC treats the early movement, the Sri Bagh Pact and the linguistic-states debate as one cluster; the Sri Bagh (1937) versus Gentlemen's (1956) pact contrast is a repeat trap.

**The story**

- The Telugu-speaking districts lay inside the **Madras Presidency**, where the Telugu elite felt overshadowed by Tamil dominance in jobs, education and politics.
- The **first Andhra Mahasabha met in 1913 at Bapatla** and formally demanded a **separate Andhra province**. A separate Andhra unit within the Congress followed in **1917**.
- Within the Andhra region itself, the less-developed **Rayalaseema** feared being dominated by the richer **Coastal Andhra**.
- The **Sri Bagh Pact (1937)** — signed at *Sri Bagh*, the Madras home of **Kasinadhuni Nageswara Rao** — reassured Rayalaseema with safeguards on **irrigation, education and the location of the capital/High Court**.
- After independence the **Dhar Commission (1948)** and the **JVP Committee (1949)** (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya) advised **against** immediate linguistic reorganisation, fearing it would threaten national unity.

**Terms explained**

- **Madras Presidency:** a large British province covering today's Tamil Nadu plus Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam-speaking areas.
- **Andhra Mahasabha:** the body/conference that led the demand for a separate Andhra province.
- **Rayalaseema / Coastal Andhra:** the two Telugu sub-regions of Madras Presidency (interior vs coast).
- **Linguistic reorganisation:** redrawing state borders so one language's speakers share one state.

**Don't confuse:** **Sri Bagh Pact (1937) = Coastal Andhra + Rayalaseema**; the later **Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) = Andhra + Telangana**. Telangana was NOT part of the early movement — it lay in princely Hyderabad State.

**Remember it:** two pacts, two pairs of regions — **Sri Bagh (1937) = Coastal + Rayalaseema; Gentlemen's (1956) = Andhra + Telangana**.

**TL;DR**

- First Andhra Mahasabha held in 1913 at Bapatla, demanding a separate Andhra province in Madras Presidency.
- Sri Bagh Pact (1937) reassured Rayalaseema against Coastal Andhra dominance, promising safeguards.
- Sri Bagh Pact signed at the Madras residence of Kasinadhuni Nageswara Rao.
- Dhar Commission (1948) and JVP Committee (1949) opposed immediate linguistic reorganisation.
keyPoints: First Andhra Mahasabha held in 1913 at Bapatla, demanding a separate Andhra province in Madras Presidency.
Sri Bagh Pact (1937) reassured Rayalaseema against Coastal Andhra dominance, promising safeguards.
Sri Bagh Pact signed at the Madras residence of Kasinadhuni Nageswara Rao.
Dhar Commission (1948) and JVP Committee (1949) opposed immediate linguistic reorganisation of states.
items.mnemonic: Two pacts, two regions: Sri Bagh (1937) = Coastal + Rayalaseema; Gentlemen's (1956) = Andhra + Telangana.
items.source: Standard accounts of the Andhra movement; Wikipedia — Sri Bagh Pact / Andhra Mahasabha

items.title: Potti Sreeramulu & the Formation of Andhra State (1952–53)
items.body:
### The fast that made a state

**In one line:** Potti Sreeramulu's death on a fast-unto-death forced the creation of Andhra State in 1953 — India's first state built on language.

**Why it is asked:** The exact 1952–53 dates (fast begins, death, Nehru's announcement, state formed) and the first/last Chief Ministers are high-frequency APPSC facts.

**The story**

- **Potti Sreeramulu** began a **fast-unto-death on 19 October 1952**, demanding a separate Andhra State for the Telugu districts of Madras State.
- He **died on 15 December 1952**. His death set off violent agitation across the Telugu districts (seven people were killed in police firing).
- On **19 December 1952**, Prime Minister **Jawaharlal Nehru** announced the formation of a separate Andhra State. Sreeramulu is remembered as **Amarajeevi** (the immortal).
- Parliament passed the **Andhra State Act in 1953**; on **1 October 1953**, **11 Telugu-speaking districts** of Madras State became **Andhra State**, with **Kurnool** as capital and the **High Court at Guntur**.

**Picture it — key offices**

| Office | Person |
|---|---|
| First Chief Minister, Andhra State | Tanguturi Prakasam ('Andhra Kesari') |
| Last Chief Minister, Andhra State | Bezawada Gopala Reddy |

**Why it matters:** Andhra State was **India's first state formed on a linguistic basis**, and its success forced the Union to set up the States Reorganisation Commission and reorganise the whole country in 1956.

**Terms explained**

- **Fast-unto-death:** refusing all food until a demand is met, risking death.
- **Amarajeevi:** 'the immortal', the honorific given to Potti Sreeramulu.
- **Andhra Kesari:** 'Lion of Andhra', the title of Tanguturi Prakasam.

**Don't confuse:** **Andhra State (1 Oct 1953, capital Kurnool)** is NOT Andhra Pradesh (1 Nov 1956, capital Hyderabad). Prakasam = first CM of **Andhra State**; Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy = first CM of **Andhra Pradesh**.

**Remember it:** '1-10-53, Kurnool' — Andhra State was born on **1 October 1953 at Kurnool**.

**TL;DR**

- Potti Sreeramulu began his final fast on 19 October 1952 and died on 15 December 1952.
- Nehru announced a separate Andhra State on 19 December 1952.
- Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as capital — India's first linguistic state.
- It comprised 11 Telugu districts of Madras State (Coastal Andhra + Rayalaseema).
- Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari) was the first CM; Bezawada Gopala Reddy the last.
keyPoints: Potti Sreeramulu began his final fast on 19 October 1952 and died on 15 December 1952.
Nehru announced a separate Andhra State on 19 December 1952.
Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as capital — India's first linguistic state.
Andhra State comprised 11 Telugu districts of Madras State (Coastal Andhra + Rayalaseema).
Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari) was the first CM; Bezawada Gopala Reddy the last.
items.mnemonic: '1-10-53, Kurnool': Andhra State born 1 Oct 1953 at Kurnool.

items.title: SRC, Gentlemen's Agreement & Birth of Andhra Pradesh (1956)
items.body:
### How Andhra State grew into Andhra Pradesh

**In one line:** In 1956 Andhra State merged with the Telugu-speaking Telangana region of Hyderabad State — after safeguards for Telangana — to form Andhra Pradesh.

**Why it is asked:** The SRC membership, the Visalandhra idea, the Gentlemen's Agreement safeguards and the 1 Nov 1956 formation are all standard questions.

**The story**

- The **States Reorganisation Commission (SRC), 1953** — chaired by **Fazl Ali**, with **H. N. Kunzru** and **K. M. Panikkar** — submitted its report in **1955**, accepting **language** as a major basis for drawing state boundaries.
- Its recommendations produced the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956** (in force 1 November 1956), backed by the **7th Constitutional Amendment**.
- The **Visalandhra** (united Telugu state) movement sought to unite all Telugu speakers — Coastal Andhra, Rayalaseema and **Telangana** (then part of Hyderabad State).
- Because Telangana was less developed, the **Gentlemen's Agreement (1956)** promised it safeguards: a **Telangana Regional Committee**, protection of Telangana's **surplus revenues**, and **domicile rules** for jobs and education.
- Andhra State merged with the **Telangana region** of Hyderabad State to form **Andhra Pradesh** on **1 November 1956**, with **Hyderabad** as capital. **Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy** became its **first Chief Minister**.

**Terms explained**

- **SRC:** States Reorganisation Commission, the body that recommended redrawing India's states by language.
- **Visalandhra:** 'Greater/United Andhra', the idea of one state for all Telugu speakers.
- **Domicile rules:** rules reserving local jobs/admissions for long-term residents of a region.
- **Regional Committee:** a legislative committee to look after a region's interests within the larger state.

**Don't confuse:** the **Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) protected Telangana**, whereas the **Sri Bagh Pact (1937) protected Rayalaseema**. The SRC was chaired by **Fazl Ali**; Kunzru and Panikkar were only members.

**Remember it:** 'FAK' SRC = **Fazl Ali, Kunzru, (Panikkar)** — the linguistic-states commission.

**TL;DR**

- SRC (1953) was chaired by Fazl Ali with members H. N. Kunzru and K. M. Panikkar; report in 1955.
- States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganised states on a linguistic basis (in force 1 Nov 1956).
- Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) gave Telangana safeguards — Regional Committee, revenue, domicile rules.
- Andhra Pradesh formed on 1 November 1956 by merging Andhra State with Telangana, capital Hyderabad.
- Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy was the first CM of Andhra Pradesh.
keyPoints: SRC (1953) was chaired by Fazl Ali with members H. N. Kunzru and K. M. Panikkar; report in 1955.
States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganised states on a linguistic basis (in force 1 Nov 1956).
Gentlemen's Agreement (1956) gave Telangana safeguards — Regional Committee, revenue, domicile rules.
Andhra Pradesh was formed on 1 November 1956 by merging Andhra State with Telangana, capital Hyderabad.
Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy was the first CM of Andhra Pradesh.
items.mnemonic: 'FAK' SRC = Fazl Ali, Kunzru, (Panikkar) — the linguistic-states commission.
items.source: Wikipedia — States Reorganisation Act, 1956; Andhra State; standard accounts of the Gentlemen's Agreement

items.title: Regional Agitations & the 2014 Bifurcation
items.body:
### From safeguards to separation

**In one line:** When Telangana's 1956 safeguards were felt to be breached, mirror-image agitations in 1969 and 1972 followed, and eventually Andhra Pradesh split in 2014.

**Why it is asked:** The 1969 vs 1972 contrast, the Mulki rules, Article 371-D and the 2014 Act dates are frequently tested, and this is a strong AP-specific Mains link.

**The story**

- Alleged breaches of the **Gentlemen's Agreement** and the **Mulki rules** (residence-based local preference for jobs and education) fed the **1969 Telangana agitation**, led by the **Telangana Praja Samithi** under **Marri Chenna Reddy**.
- When the **Supreme Court upheld the Mulki rules in 1972**, Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema launched the **Jai Andhra movement (1972)** demanding a separate Andhra state.
- The **Six-Point Formula (1973)** resolved both agitations and was given effect through **Article 371-D** (32nd Amendment), providing equitable education and employment across regions.
- The Telangana demand revived strongly after 2000 under the **Telangana Rashtra Samithi (K. Chandrashekar Rao)**; the **Srikrishna Committee (2010)** examined it. The causes commonly cited were three: a **perceived violation of the safeguards** promised in the Gentlemen's Agreement; the **concentration of development around Hyderabad**; and **grievances over water** (Krishna–Godavari irrigation), **jobs and educational opportunities**.
- The **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014**, passed by Parliament in February 2014 (Lok Sabha 18 Feb, Rajya Sabha 20 Feb, assent 1 March 2014) fixed **2 June 2014** as the **appointed day**: **Telangana** became India's **29th state**.
- **Hyderabad** was made the **common capital for up to ten years**; **Amaravati** was planned as the capital of residuary Andhra Pradesh.

**Picture it — the two agitations**

| Movement | Year | Region | Trigger |
|---|---|---|---|
| Telangana agitation | 1969 | Telangana | Breach of Mulki rules/safeguards |
| Jai Andhra | 1972 | Coastal Andhra + Rayalaseema | Supreme Court upheld Mulki rules |

**Terms explained**

- **Mulki rules:** rules reserving local government jobs/admissions for long-term residents (e.g. 15 years in Hyderabad).
- **Article 371-D:** a special constitutional provision for equitable jobs/education across AP's regions.
- **Appointed day:** the date on which a reorganisation legally takes effect.
- **Bifurcation:** splitting one state into two.

**Don't confuse:** **1969 = Telangana** wanted OUT; **1972 Jai Andhra = Coastal Andhra/Rayalaseema** reacting to the Mulki-rules verdict. **Six-Point Formula (1973) → Article 371-D**, not Article 370.

**Remember it:** '2-6-14, 29' — Telangana was born on **2 June 2014 as the 29th state**.

**TL;DR**

- Mulki rules gave residence-based preference for local jobs/education; their breach fed the 1969 Telangana agitation.
- 1969 Telangana movement led by Telangana Praja Samithi under Marri Chenna Reddy.
- Jai Andhra movement (1972) followed the Supreme Court upholding the Mulki rules.
- Six-Point Formula (1973) was implemented via Article 371-D (32nd Amendment).
- AP Reorganisation Act 2014: appointed day 2 June 2014; Telangana became the 29th state.
- Hyderabad = common capital for up to 10 years; Amaravati = residuary AP capital.

Causes of the separate-Telangana demand: perceived violation of Gentlemen's Agreement safeguards, development concentrated around Hyderabad, grievances over water, jobs and education.

items.title: District Reorganisation of AP (2014 → 2026)
items.body:
### How many districts AP has now

**In one line:** Residuary Andhra Pradesh grew from 13 districts in 2014 to 26 in 2022 and 28 at the end of 2025.

**Why it is asked:** This is live, current-affairs-style AP factual material; the exact count and the two newest districts are the kind of 'as of now' facts APPSC loves, and a common trap is the outdated '26 districts'.

**Picture it — evolution of districts**

| Date | Districts | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 2 Jun 2014 | 13 | Residuary AP at bifurcation |
| 4 Apr 2022 | 26 | Wholesale reorganisation |
| 31 Dec 2025 | 28 | +Polavaram, +Markapuram |

**The story — the two newest districts (31 Dec 2025):**

- **Polavaram** — headquarters **Rampachodavaram**; carved from Alluri Sitharama Raju district; it is AP's **least populous** district.
- **Markapuram** — headquarters Markapuram; carved from Prakasam district.

**Don't confuse:** **Madanapalle is NOT a district** — it is the **headquarters of Annamayya district**. (A November 2025 '29 districts' proposal was not notified.) AP now has **28** districts, not the outdated 26.

**Remember it:** 28 districts since 31 Dec 2025; the two newest spell 'P-M' = **Polavaram (Rampachodavaram)** and **Markapuram**.

**Terms explained**

- **Zilla parishad:** the elected district-level rural local-government body; AP's **28 zilla parishads** take effect from **25 September 2026**.
- **Residuary Andhra Pradesh:** the part of the old state left after Telangana was separated in 2014.

**TL;DR**

- AP has 28 districts since 31 December 2025 (was 26 from 4 April 2022, 13 in 2014).
- The two 2025 additions are Polavaram (HQ Rampachodavaram) and Markapuram (HQ Markapuram).
- Polavaram is AP's least populous district; Madanapalle is the HQ of Annamayya district, not a district.
- 28 zilla parishads take effect from 25 September 2026.
keyPoints: AP has 28 districts since 31 December 2025 (was 26 from 4 April 2022, 13 in 2014).
The two 2025 additions are Polavaram (HQ Rampachodavaram) and Markapuram (HQ Markapuram).
Polavaram is AP's least populous district; Madanapalle is the HQ of Annamayya district, not a district.

items.title: From Bapatla to Swami Sitaram — the Andhra Movement 1913–1951
items.body:
### From Bapatla to Swami Sitaram — the Andhra Movement 1913–1951

**In one line**
Four decades of conferences, a university, a pact between two regions and one failed fast before Potti Sriramulu.

**The story**
The demand dates from **1911**–12. The first Andhra Mahasabha met at Bapatla under **Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma** (1913), and the second at Bezawada under **Nyapati Subba Rao** (1914). The **Nagpur** Congress (1920) gave Andhra its own Congress unit. **Andhra University** followed in **1926**, with **C.R. Reddy** as Vice-Chancellor. At **Nandyal** in 1928 **Chilukuri Narayana Rao** renamed the Ceded Districts 'Rayalaseema'. Rayalaseema feared the richer coast. The Sri Bagh Pact of **16 November 1937**, signed by Pattabhi, **Kadapa Koti Reddy** and others, promised a university centre at **Anantapur** and irrigation priority (**Tungabhadra**, Krishna–Pennar). It let Rayalaseema choose either the capital or the **High Court**, and divided seats **district-wise**. In **1938** the Madras Assembly passed **Konda Venkatappayya**'s resolution for an Andhra province. After independence the JVP Report demanded that the Andhras give up **Madras city**, and the **Partition Committee** (1949) deadlocked. **Swami Sitaram**'s 35-day fast (1951) ended on **Vinoba** Bhave's appeal.

#### 1911–1951

| Event | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Bapatla, 1913** | First Andhra Mahasabha, 26 May 1913 — president **Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma** |
| **Bezawada, 1914** | Second conference — **Nyapati Subba Rao** Pantulu |
| **Beginning** | Demand first raised **1911**–12 |
| **Congress principle** | **Nagpur** session 1920 — Congress circles by language |
| **Andhra University** | **1926** — Bezawada → Waltair (1930); first VC **C.R. Reddy** |
| **"Rayalaseema"** | Coined by **Chilukuri Narayana Rao**, **Nandyal**, 1928 |
| **1938 resolution** | Moved by **Konda Venkatappayya** — Andhra & Kerala provinces |
| **JVP condition** | Andhra possible — if the claim to **Madras city** was dropped |
| **Partition Committee (1949)** | Madras govt body on separation — deadlocked; Prakasam dissented |
| **Swami Sitaram (1951)** | 35-day fast; ended at **Vinoba** Bhave's appeal |

#### Sri Bagh Pact (1937)

| Clause | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Date** | **16 November 1937** |
| **Signatories** | Pattabhi Sitaramayya, **Kadapa Koti Reddy**, Konda Venkatappayya and others |
| **Education** | University centre at **Anantapur** |
| **Irrigation** | Priority for Rayalaseema — **Tungabhadra**, Krishna–Pennar (10 years) |
| **Capital / High Court** | Rayalaseema chooses capital or **High Court**; coast gets the other |
| **Seats** | Assembly seats **district-wise**, equal between regions |

**Don't confuse**
- **Bapatla 1913** (Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma) ≠ **Bezawada 1914** (Nyapati Subba Rao).
- **Swami Sitaram's fast (1951)** was called off; **Potti Sriramulu's fast (1952)** ended in death and statehood.
- The PYQ bank dates the Gentlemen's Agreement to 1 Nov 1956 (when it took effect); it was **signed on 20 February 1956**.

**TL;DR**
- 1911 demand; Bapatla 1913 (Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma); Bezawada 1914 (Nyapati Subba Rao); Nagpur Congress 1920.
- Andhra University 1926 (C.R. Reddy); "Rayalaseema" coined at Nandyal 1928 (Chilukuri Narayana Rao).
- Sri Bagh 16 Nov 1937: Anantapur university centre, Tungabhadra priority, capital-or-High-Court choice, district-wise seats.
- 1938 resolution (Konda Venkatappayya); JVP 1949 — give up Madras city; Partition Committee 1949; Swami Sitaram 1951.
keyPoints: The first Andhra Mahasabha (Bapatla, 1913) was presided over by Bayya Narasimheswara Sarma.
Chilukuri Narayana Rao coined the name 'Rayalaseema' at Nandyal in 1928.
The Sri Bagh Pact was signed on 16 November 1937.
Under the Sri Bagh Pact Rayalaseema could choose between the capital and the High Court.
Swami Sitaram fasted for 35 days in 1951 and stopped at Vinoba Bhave's appeal.

items.title: Potti Sriramulu and Andhra State, 1952–56 — Detail
items.body:
### Potti Sriramulu and Andhra State, 1952–56 — Detail

**In one line**
The man behind the fast, the inquiry that priced the new state, and the people who ran it at Kurnool.

**The story**
Potti Sriramulu was born on **16 March 1901** in Madras, to a family from **Padamatipalli** in Nellore. A Gandhian, he had already fasted in 1946 for Dalit entry into the **Venugopalaswamy** temple at **Nellore**. In 1952 he fasted at **Bulusu Sambamurthy**'s house in **Mylapore** for **58 days** until his death. Nellore district now bears his name — **Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore**. After Nehru's announcement, Justice K.N. **Wanchoo** reported on the new state's finances. Nehru **inaugurated** Andhra State at Kurnool on 1 October 1953. **C.M. Trivedi** was its Governor and **Koka Subba Rao** first Chief Justice at Guntur. Its 11 districts ran from Srikakulam to **Cuddapah** and **Chittoor**. **Bellary** town went to Mysore. Prakasam's ministry fell by **one vote** in 1954, and Bezawada Gopala Reddy won the **1955** mid-term poll. **Nallapati Venkatramaiah** was the first Speaker.

#### Andhra State

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Birth** | **16 March 1901**, Madras; family from **Padamatipalli** (Nellore) |
| **Earlier fast (1946)** | Dalit entry into the **Venugopalaswamy** temple, **Nellore** |
| **Venue** | **Bulusu Sambamurthy**'s house, **Mylapore**, Madras |
| **Length** | **58 days** (some sources 56) |
| **Memorial** | District renamed **Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore** (2008) |
| **Wanchoo Committee** | Justice K.N. **Wanchoo** — finances & administration of the new state (1953 report) |
| **1 Oct 1953** | Nehru **inaugurated** Andhra State at Kurnool |
| **Governor** | **C.M. Trivedi** — first Governor (Andhra State, then AP) |
| **High Court** | Guntur, July 1954 — CJ **Koka Subba Rao** |
| **11 districts** | Srikakulam … Nellore, Kurnool, Anantapur, **Cuddapah**, **Chittoor** |
| **Bellary** | Town went to Mysore (Misra report, 1953) |
| **1954–55** | Prakasam fell by **one vote** (Nov 1954); mid-term poll **1955** → Gopala Reddy |
| **Speaker** | **Nallapati Venkatramaiah** (Andhra State) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Wanchoo Committee** (1953) = finances of Andhra State; **Wanchoo** ≠ **Srikrishna** (2010, Telangana).
- **C.M. Trivedi** was Governor of both Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956).

**TL;DR**
- Potti Sriramulu: b. 16 Mar 1901; 1946 Nellore temple-entry fast; 1952 fast at Bulusu Sambamurthy's house, Mylapore, 58 days.
- Nellore renamed Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore (2008).
- Wanchoo Committee; inaugurated by Nehru at Kurnool; Governor C.M. Trivedi; CJ Koka Subba Rao (Guntur).
- Bellary to Mysore; Prakasam fell by one vote (1954); Gopala Reddy CM 1955; Speaker Nallapati Venkatramaiah.

**Don’t confuse (what each item stands for)**
- **Potti Sriramulu’s 1946 fast** was for **temple entry for Dalits at the Venugopalaswamy temple, Nellore** — not for statehood; his 1952 fast (58 days, died 15 Dec 1952) was for Andhra State.
- The **Wanchoo Committee** was appointed to work out the **implications of forming Andhra State** (assets, personnel and boundaries).
- **Andhra State (1 Oct 1953)** was formed of **eleven districts — seven coastal and four Rayalaseema** (Rayalaseema: Kurnool, Anantapur, **Cuddapah** and **Chittoor**), with Kurnool as capital.
keyPoints: Potti Sriramulu fasted at Bulusu Sambamurthy's house in Mylapore, Madras.
His 1952 fast lasted 58 days.
Justice K.N. Wanchoo examined the implications of forming Andhra State.
C.M. Trivedi was the first Governor of Andhra State.
Potti Sriramulu’s 1946 fast was for temple entry at the Venugopalaswamy temple, Nellore; the Wanchoo Committee studied the implications of forming Andhra State.
Andhra State 1953 had eleven districts: seven coastal and four Rayalaseema — Kurnool, Anantapur, Cuddapah and Chittoor.

items.title: Visalandhra, the SRC and the Gentlemen's Agreement — Detail
items.body:
### Visalandhra, the SRC and the Gentlemen's Agreement — Detail

**In one line**
How the Telugu areas of Hyderabad joined Andhra State, and the safeguards written for them.

**The story**
The Communists had argued for a united Telugu state since **Visalandhralo Prajarajyam** (1946) by P. Sundarayya. The SRC was cautious. It advised keeping Telangana a separate Hyderabad State until after the **1961** elections, merging only if **two-thirds** of its legislators agreed. Hyderabad's Chief Minister **Burgula Ramakrishna Rao** and the Andhra leaders pressed for immediate merger. The **Gentlemen's Agreement** of **20 February 1956** was signed by four leaders from each side — among them **Gouthu Latchanna** and **K.V. Ranga Reddy**. It promised a **Deputy Chief Minister** from the other region, and job preference after **12 years** of residence. A Telangana regional council was later set up as the **Regional Committee** (1958, Article **371**). These rules sat on top of the Nizam's Mulki rules of **1919** (**15 years**' residence). Nehru blessed the union as a '**matrimonial alliance**' with a right to divorce. AP began with **20 districts**, and **Kaleswara Rao** became Speaker. The **Pataskar** award (in force 1960) settled the Madras border: **Tiruttani** went to Madras.

#### 1956

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Communist case** | P. Sundarayya — '**Visalandhralo Prajarajyam**' (1946) |
| **SRC on Telangana** | Keep Hyderabad State separate; merge after **1961** if **two-thirds** of its MLAs agree |
| **Hyderabad CM** | **Burgula Ramakrishna Rao** (1952–56) — backed Visalandhra |
| **Gentlemen's Agreement** | Signed, Delhi, **20 February 1956** |
| **Signatories** | Andhra: Gopala Reddy, Sanjeeva Reddy, **Gouthu Latchanna**, A. Satyanarayana Raju; Telangana: Burgula, **K.V. Ranga Reddy**, Chenna Reddy, J.V. Narsing Rao |
| **Clause — leadership** | CM from one region → **Deputy Chief Minister** from the other |
| **Clause — domicile** | **12 years**' residence for Telangana jobs |
| **Clause — Regional body** | Telangana **Regional Committee** (1958 Order under Art **371**) |
| **Mulki rules** | Nizam's firman **1919** — **15 years** of residence |
| **Nehru's remark** | A '**matrimonial alliance**' with provision for divorce |
| **AP in 1956** | **20 districts** — 11 Andhra + 9 Telangana |
| **AP Speaker** | Ayyadevara **Kaleswara Rao** (1956) |
| **AP–Madras border** | **Pataskar** award — **Tiruttani** to Madras (in force 1960) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mulki rules** (Nizam, 1919): **15 years**; **Gentlemen's Agreement** domicile: **12 years**.
- **Sri Bagh (1937)**: Coastal–Rayalaseema; **Gentlemen's (1956)**: Andhra–Telangana; **Six-Point Formula (1973)**: whole state.

**TL;DR**
- Visalandhralo Prajarajyam (P. Sundarayya, 1946); SRC: Telangana separate till 1961, merger on two-thirds consent.
- Gentlemen's Agreement 20 Feb 1956: 4 + 4 signatories (Gouthu Latchanna, K.V. Ranga Reddy …); Deputy CM clause; 12 years' residence.
- Regional Committee 1958 (Art 371); Mulki rules 1919 (15 years).
- Nehru: 'matrimonial alliance'; 20 districts in 1956; Speaker Kaleswara Rao; Pataskar award — Tiruttani to Madras.
keyPoints: The SRC recommended that Telangana remain separate until the 1961 elections.
The Gentlemen's Agreement was signed on 20 February 1956.
Under the Gentlemen's Agreement the Deputy Chief Minister was to come from the other region.
Nehru called the 1956 merger a 'matrimonial alliance'.

items.title: The 1969 and 1972 Agitations and the 1973–75 Settlement — Detail
items.body:
### The 1969 and 1972 Agitations and the 1973–75 Settlement — Detail

**In one line**
Two agitations from opposite directions, ended by a formula that was written into the Constitution.

**The story**
The 1969 Telangana agitation began at **Khammam** with a student's fast. Indira Gandhi's **Eight-Point** Plan did not stop it. In 1971 the Telangana Praja Samithi won **10 of the 14** Lok Sabha seats in the region, then merged into the Congress, and P.V. **Narasimha Rao** became Chief Minister. On **3 October 1972** the Supreme Court upheld the Mulki rules. Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema rose in the Jai Andhra movement; minister **Kakani Venkataratnam** died during it. Narasimha Rao resigned, and **President's Rule** followed for most of **1973**. The Six-Point Formula of **21 September 1973** was written into the 32nd Amendment as Article 371-D. The same amendment added **371-E**, under which the **University of Hyderabad** was founded. The **Presidential Order** of **1975** replaced the Mulki rules with local cadres in **six zones**. When non-locals kept getting Telangana posts, G.O. **610** (1985) ordered them sent back, and the **Girglani** Commission later found the order flouted.

#### 1969–2001

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Spark (1969)** | Student Ravindranath's fast at **Khammam** |
| **April 1969** | Indira Gandhi's **Eight-Point** Plan |
| **1971 election** | TPS won **10 of the 14** Telangana Lok Sabha seats |
| **P.V. Narasimha Rao** | CM 1971 → resigned Jan 1973 (Jai Andhra) |
| **Mulki verdict** | Supreme Court, **3 October 1972** |
| **Jai Andhra leader** | **Kakani Venkataratnam** — died Dec 1972 |
| **President's Rule** | Jan–Dec **1973** |
| **Six-Point Formula** | **21 September 1973** |
| **32nd Amendment** | Art 371-D + **371-E** → central **University of Hyderabad** (1974) |
| **Presidential Order 1975** | Local cadres, **six zones**; Mulki rules repealed |
| **G.O. 610** | 1985 — repatriation of non-locals; **Girglani** Commission 2001 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Article 371-D** = equitable jobs and education (Six-Point Formula); **371-E** = a central university in AP (University of Hyderabad).
- **Eight-Point Plan (1969)** failed; **Six-Point Formula (1973)** succeeded.

**TL;DR**
- 1969: began at Khammam; Eight-Point Plan; TPS won 10 of 14 LS seats (1971).
- P.V. Narasimha Rao CM 1971–73; SC upheld Mulki rules 3 Oct 1972; Jai Andhra — Kakani Venkataratnam.
- President's Rule 1973; Six-Point Formula 21 Sept 1973; 32nd Amendment → 371-D and 371-E (University of Hyderabad).
- Presidential Order 1975 (six zones); G.O. 610 (1985); Girglani Commission (2001).

**Don’t confuse (agitations and safeguards)**
- The **1969 Telangana agitation began at Khammam**, with student **Ravindranath’s fast**.
- **Jai Andhra (1972–73)** brought down Chief Minister **P. V. Narasimha Rao**, who resigned in **January 1973**.
- **President’s Rule in Andhra Pradesh ran from January to December 1973**.
- The **Presidential Order of 1975** set up **local cadres and six zones** for recruitment.
keyPoints: The Supreme Court upheld the Mulki rules on 3 October 1972.
Kakani Venkataratnam led the Jai Andhra movement.
The Six-Point Formula was announced on 21 September 1973.
Article 371-E led to the University of Hyderabad.
The 1975 Presidential Order created six zones for employment.
The 1969 Telangana agitation began at Khammam with student Ravindranath’s fast; Jai Andhra forced P. V. Narasimha Rao to resign in January 1973.
President’s Rule in AP ran January to December 1973; the 1975 Presidential Order created local cadres and six zones.

items.title: From TRS to the Common Capital's End, 2001–2024 — Detail
items.body:
### From TRS to the Common Capital's End, 2001–2024 — Detail

**In one line**
The second Telangana movement, the 2014 Act, and the long argument over the capital of the residuary state.

**The story**
KCR launched the TRS on **27 April 2001**. His fast of November 2009 led Home Minister Chidambaram to announce, on **9 December 2009**, that Telangana would be formed. A backlash in the other regions forced a pause. The Srikrishna Committee reported on **30 December 2010** with **six options**, and the Congress Working Committee decided on **30 July 2013**. United AP's last Chief Minister, **Kiran Kumar Reddy**, resigned in protest. After 2 June 2014 KCR led Telangana, and Chandrababu Naidu took charge of residuary AP on **8 June 2014**. To build Polavaram — declared a **national project** — **seven mandals** of Khammam were moved to AP. Modi laid Amaravati's foundation at **Uddandarayunipalem** on **22 October 2015**, and AP got its own High Court on **1 January 2019**. The 2020 three-capitals plan (with **Kurnool (judicial)**) was **repealed** in 2021. Hyderabad stopped being the common capital on **2 June 2024**.

#### 2001–2024

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **TRS** | Founded by KCR, **27 April 2001** |
| **2009** | KCR fast 29 Nov; Chidambaram announcement **9 December 2009** |
| **Srikrishna Committee** | Report **30 December 2010** — **six options** |
| **CWC resolution** | **30 July 2013** |
| **Last CM of united AP** | N. **Kiran Kumar Reddy** (resigned Feb 2014) |
| **First CMs** | Telangana: KCR (2 June); residuary AP: Chandrababu Naidu (**8 June 2014**) |
| **Polavaram mandals** | **Seven mandals** of Khammam → AP (2014) |
| **Polavaram** | Declared a **national project** by the 2014 Act |
| **Amaravati** | Foundation stone, **Uddandarayunipalem**, **22 October 2015** |
| **AP High Court** | Separate court at Amaravati from **1 January 2019** |
| **Three-capitals Act (2020)** | Visakhapatnam exec, Amaravati legis, **Kurnool (judicial)**; **repealed** Nov 2021 |
| **Common capital ends** | **2 June 2024** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Srikrishna Committee (2010)** — six options; **Wanchoo Committee (1953)** — finances of Andhra State.
- The **three-capitals Act** (2020) was **repealed** (2021); Amaravati remains the capital, Hyderabad's common-capital term ended **2 June 2024**.

**TL;DR**
- TRS 27 April 2001; Chidambaram announcement 9 Dec 2009; Srikrishna report 30 Dec 2010 (six options); CWC 30 July 2013.
- Last CM of united AP Kiran Kumar Reddy; first CMs — KCR (Telangana), Naidu (AP, 8 June 2014).
- Polavaram national project; seven Khammam mandals to AP; Amaravati foundation 22 Oct 2015 (Uddandarayunipalem).
- AP High Court 1 Jan 2019; three-capitals Act 2020, repealed 2021; common capital ended 2 June 2024.
keyPoints: The Srikrishna Committee (2010) gave six options.
N. Kiran Kumar Reddy was the last Chief Minister of united Andhra Pradesh.
The AP Reorganisation Act 2014 declared Polavaram a national project.
Amaravati's foundation stone was laid on 22 October 2015.
Hyderabad ceased to be the common capital on 2 June 2024.

items.title: For Mains — Andhra Movement & Formation of Andhra Pradesh
items.body:
This topic feeds **Mains Paper-II** on two clauses: **M2-9** ('Andhra nationalist movement — Justice Party, revolutionary literature, Andhra Mahasabhas, Potti Sriramulu') and **M2-10** ('AP Bifurcation impacts, new capital, employees, river water, Reorganization Act'). Mains wants a **thesis with a long arc** — how linguistic identity first built, then strained, and finally split the Telugu state.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Origins | Tamil dominance in Madras Presidency; Andhra Mahasabha (1913); sub-regional balance (Sri Bagh Pact 1937) |
| Breakthrough | Potti Sreeramulu's sacrifice; Andhra State 1953 as India's first linguistic state; the SRC it forced |
| Union & its strains | Visalandhra ideal; Gentlemen's Agreement safeguards; 1969 and 1972 agitations; Article 371-D |
| Bifurcation (2014) | Causes (uneven development, water, jobs); AP Reorganisation Act; appointed day 2 June 2014 |
| Bifurcation impacts | New capital (Amaravati), employee allocation, river-water sharing (Krishna–Godavari), revenue deficit |
| Way forward | Equitable regional development; cooperative federalism; resolving capital and water disputes |

**Data points / committees to quote:** Andhra Mahasabha (1913, Bapatla); Sri Bagh Pact (1937); Potti Sreeramulu (died 15 Dec 1952); Andhra State (1 Oct 1953); SRC/Fazl Ali (16 states + 3 UTs); Gentlemen's Agreement (1956); Six-Point Formula (1973) → Article 371-D; Srikrishna Committee (2010); AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (Telangana = 29th state); AP now has 28 districts (31 Dec 2025).

**AP angle:** this entire topic IS the AP angle — use it to show APPSC-level command of the state's political formation, and connect the bifurcation's unfinished agenda (capital at Amaravati, river-water disputes, revenue deficit) to current AP governance debates.

**Use in answers:** frame the arc 'identity built it (1953/1956) → inequity strained it (1969/1972) → inequity split it (2014)'; quote the Gentlemen's Agreement and Article 371-D; close with the bifurcation's unresolved issues. A timeline diagram (1913 → 1953 → 1956 → 1973 → 2014 → 2025) is a strong visual.
keyPoints: Serves Mains Paper-II clauses M2-9 (Andhra nationalist movement) and M2-10 (bifurcation impacts).
Arc: identity built the state (1953/1956), inequity strained it (1969/1972), inequity split it (2014).
Quote: Sri Bagh Pact (1937), Gentlemen's Agreement (1956), Article 371-D, Srikrishna Committee (2010).
Bifurcation impacts: Amaravati capital, employee allocation, Krishna–Godavari water, revenue deficit.
This is the core AP topic — link to current governance debates (capital, water).
